artiest/the-isley-brothers.text:
The Isley Brothers are an American soul group from Cincinnati, Ohio. In 1954 four young brothers began as a gospel group: O'Kelly, Rudolph, Ronald and Vernon. Vernon was killed in an accident that year and the rest stopped for a while. Later Ronald, Rudolph and O'Kelly formed a trio again. In the late 1950s they moved to New York, where they broke through in 1959 with Shout, written by the brothers themselves. The record blended gospel singing with doo-wop harmonies.

In the 1960s they recorded for various labels. Twist and Shout reached the top twenty and This Old Heart of Mine (Is Weak for You) was released on Motown. In 1969, on their own label T-Neck Records, they made It's Your Thing, which won a Grammy. In 1973 the younger brothers Ernie and Marvin and brother-in-law Chris Jasper joined, turning the trio into a full band. The years that followed were the commercial peak, with albums such as 3+3, The Heat Is On and Between the Sheets. The Heat Is On reached number one on the Billboard 200.

With new work the group managed to reach the Billboard Hot 100 in six different decades, from the 1950s to the 2000s, which no other group has done. In 1992 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and in 2014 they received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. Through their long career, from gospel to funk, the Isley Brothers let us hear the development of American black music over more than fifty years.
artiest/the-isley-brothers.listen: Listen to Shout and notice the singing. Can you hear the gospel in the way the song is sung?

artiest/the-jackson-5.text:
The Jackson 5 was a family group from Gary, Indiana, started in 1964 by father Joe Jackson with his sons Jackie, Tito and Jermaine. Soon afterwards Marlon and the five-year-old Michael joined as well. The brothers won talent contests in Gary and Chicago and in 1967 also at the Apollo Theater in New York. After a first record deal with the small Steeltown Records, singer Bobby Taylor arranged an audition at Motown in 1968, and Berry Gordy signed the group. Michael soon became the lead singer.

Gordy sent the brothers to Hollywood and set up a special songwriting and production team, The Corporation. Their first Motown single, I Want You Back, was released in October 1969 and reached number 1 in America in January 1970. ABC, The Love You Save and I'll Be There followed: the first four singles all reached number one. The debut album was called Diana Ross Presents the Jackson 5. In 1975 the group left Motown for Epic, where they continued as The Jacksons, with Randy in place of Jermaine.

The Jackson 5 made cheerful, danceable soul and pop for a young audience, with Michael's clear boyish voice out in front and the harmonies of his brothers behind it. They were among the first black artists with a large audience across several genres. Motown sold posters, stickers and even a cartoon series: in effect this was one of the first boy bands. Michael later grew into one of the biggest solo stars in pop history.
artiest/the-jackson-5.listen: Listen to I Want You Back and notice the piano glissando at the start and the nimble bass line that drives the whole song. Hear how the brothers answer Michael's lead vocal with short responses.

artiest/the-jazz-composer-s-orchestra.text:
The Jazz Composer's Orchestra was an American jazz group, founded in 1965 by Carla Bley and Michael Mantler to perform avant-garde jazz for large orchestra. Its roots lie in the Jazz Composers Guild, an organisation of Bill Dixon that grew out of the 1964 concert series October Revolution in Jazz in New York. There Bley and Mantler formed a big band, first called the Jazz Composers Guild Orchestra, which recorded its first record in April 1965. When the Guild fell apart, the big band continued as the Jazz Composer's Orchestra. In 1966 a non-profit organisation was added, the Jazz Composers Orchestra Association.

The first release was Communication, in 1965. The double album The Jazz Composer's Orchestra from 1968 featured soloists such as Cecil Taylor, Don Cherry, Roswell Rudd, Pharoah Sanders, Larry Coryell and Gato Barbieri. Later followed, among others, Numatik Swing Band, Relativity Suite, Echoes of Prayer, For Players Only and The Gardens of Harlem. For the records the group founded the label JCOA Records, and there were commissioned works by among others Roswell Rudd, Clifford Thornton, Don Cherry, Leroy Jenkins and Grachan Moncur III.

The last performance was in 1975. The orchestra's activities led to a distribution company for records of its own, the New Music Distribution Service. In this way the orchestra gave room not only to the new jazz, but also to the musicians who wanted to release their own records outside the major labels.
artiest/the-jazz-composer-s-orchestra.listen: Listen to the album The Jazz Composer's Orchestra from 1968 and notice the interplay between the large orchestra and the soloists. Can you hear when a soloist is given room?

artiest/the-jimi-hendrix-experience.text:
The Jimi Hendrix Experience was the band around the American guitarist and singer Jimi Hendrix, born in 1942 in Seattle. Hendrix began playing guitar at the age of fifteen, joined the army in 1961 and was discharged a year later. He then played on the Chitlin' Circuit and in the backing bands of among others the Isley Brothers and Little Richard. At the end of 1966 he moved to England, where Chas Chandler of The Animals became his manager. Within a few months he formed the Experience, with bassist Noel Redding and drummer Mitch Mitchell.

The group had three top ten hits in the United Kingdom: Hey Joe, Purple Haze and The Wind Cries Mary. In 1967 Are You Experienced was released, and in the same year Axis: Bold as Love. The performance at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 made Hendrix famous in the United States. The third album, Electric Ladyland from 1968, was his greatest success and his only number one on the American album chart. Hendrix played at Woodstock in 1969 and at the Isle of Wight Festival in 1970. He died in London in September 1970, at the age of twenty-seven.

Hendrix used heavily amplified, overdriven guitar amplifiers and made feedback a musical tool. He was also one of the first guitarists to use effects such as fuzz, Octavia, wah-wah and Uni-Vibe on a large scale, and the first to put stereo phasing effects on record. In this way he turned the electric guitar into a source of electronic sound. In 1992 the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-jimi-hendrix-experience.listen: Listen to Purple Haze by The Jimi Hendrix Experience. Notice the chord the song begins with, a dominant chord in which the major and minor third are heard at the same time, and the twisted, distorted guitar sound.

artiest/the-john-barry-seven.text:
The John Barry Seven was an English rock and roll band, formed in 1957 by John Barry after he had left his original path as an arranger for big bands. He asked three musicians he had served with in the army and three local musicians. The first line-up consisted of Barry himself on vocals and trumpet, two saxophonists, a drummer, a bassist and two guitarists. In 1957 and 1958 the band took part in British TV programmes such as Six-Five Special and Oh Boy!, a demanding programme under Jack Good. Because of the heavy rehearsals and touring, the atmosphere in the group came under strain, and almost the entire line-up left.

In 1958 lead guitarist Vic Flick joined, later also known for his work with Barry. For the BBC programme Drumbeat, intended as a rival to Oh Boy!, the band was expanded with pianist Les Reed. In 1961 Barry was too busy arranging and composing, after which Flick took over the leadership and Bobby Carr played trumpet. The group had a few hits in England, such as Hit and Miss, which reached number ten on the British chart in 1960 and was the theme tune of Juke Box Jury. They often toured with Adam Faith.

Barry himself focused on compositions and arrangements. The James Bond Theme reached number 13 in England in 1962, under the name The John Barry Orchestra. In this way the group stands at the beginning of one of the best-known careers in film music.
artiest/the-john-barry-seven.listen: Listen to Hit and Miss and notice the electric guitar and the horns. Can you hear why this song could work as the theme music of a TV programme?

artiest/the-jolly-boys.text:
The Jolly Boys is a mento band from Port Antonio in Jamaica. Mento is the traditional Jamaican music that preceded ska and reggae. The group grew out of the Navy Island Swamp Boys, founded in 1945 and often heard at Errol Flynn's parties. When that band broke up in 1955, Moses Deans and Papa Brown founded the Jolly Boys, reportedly with a name devised by Flynn. The band played in hotels and at private parties and was regarded as the best mento band in the region. In 1962 it was a finalist in a national mento competition in Kingston.

In 1989 producer Jules Shear heard the band in a hotel and decided to make an album. This is how Pop 'n' Mento came about. Between 1989 and 1997 four albums were released, including Sunshine 'n' Water in 1991 and Beer Joint & Tailoring in 1992. The records led to world tours and to a part in the film The Mighty Quinn. In 2010 Great Expectation was released, with rock covers in mento style, featuring singer Albert Minott.

In mento one hears banjo, guitar, maracas and the rumba box, a large thumb piano that plays the bass. This makes the music lighter and more rhythmic than reggae. The Jolly Boys show that Jamaica had a musical history that began long before reggae.
artiest/the-jolly-boys.listen: Listen to Touch Me Tomato and notice the rumba box, which plays the bass. Can you also hear the banjo and the maracas that set the tempo?

artiest/the-killers.text:
The Killers are an American rock band from Las Vegas, formed in 2001 by Brandon Flowers (vocals, keyboards, bass) and guitarist Dave Keuning. Flowers had been thrown out of his first band, a synth-pop trio, and after an Oasis concert decided that he wanted to play in a rock band. He answered an advertisement from Keuning. At their first meeting Keuning gave him a tape with an early riff of Mr. Brightside, and the next time Flowers came back with lyrics and melody. The name comes from a fictional band in the video for Crystal by New Order. In 2002 bassist Mark Stoermer and drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr. joined.

In Las Vegas, where punk, nu metal and rap dominated, the group stood out with a blend of British pop styles and lo-fi indie rock. The debut album Hot Fuss was released in 2004. Sam's Town followed in 2006, Day & Age in 2008, Battle Born in 2012, Wonderful Wonderful in 2017, Imploding the Mirage in 2020 and Pressure Machine in 2021. Each of those seven albums reached the top of the British album chart. They have performed in more than fifty countries, including at Madison Square Garden, Wembley and at Glastonbury in 2007 and 2019.

The Killers sound like a guitar band with a synthesizer at its heart: danceable rhythms, rousing choruses and a voice that is allowed to be theatrical. They show how the British post-punk and synth-pop of the 1980s came back in the rock of the twenty-first century. The group is seen as one of the biggest rock bands of our time.
artiest/the-killers.listen: Listen to Mr. Brightside by The Killers. Notice the fast guitar riff that keeps returning, and how the chorus pushes the tempo and tension up even further.

artiest/the-king-s-consort.text:
The King's Consort is a British early-music orchestra, founded in 1980 by conductor and harpsichordist Robert King, who was born in Wombourne in 1960. The orchestra is accompanied by the Choir of The King's Consort. Together they have made more than a hundred recordings. From 1987 to 2007 ninety albums were released on the Hyperion label, followed by thirteen more on their own label Vivat, together selling more than one and a half million CDs. The ensemble gives concert seasons in England and tours internationally.

The repertoire comes mainly from the Baroque and early Classical periods, but also includes nineteenth-century work and commissions for contemporary composers such as Michael Finnissy and Michael Berkeley. Their regular London base has been the Wigmore Hall since 1987. The orchestra has played at the BBC Proms seven times, first in 1991 with Handel's Music for the Royal Fireworks. Among the recordings are Handel, Bach, Vivaldi and Mozart, as shown by albums such as The Four Seasons (1989), Joshua (1991) and the series Complete Odes and Welcome Songs.

The choir can also be heard on the soundtracks of films such as The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, Kingdom of Heaven, Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest and The Da Vinci Code. In 2006 the ensemble won a BBC Music Magazine Choral Award for the Requiem by Michael Haydn. In this way The King's Consort brought the music of the Baroque to a wide audience, through the concert hall and through the cinema.
artiest/the-king-s-consort.listen: Listen to The Four Seasons in the performance by The King's Consort and notice the sound of the instruments and the way the orchestra makes spring, summer, autumn and winter differ. Which season do you recognise first?

artiest/the-kings-of-rhythm.text:
Kings of Rhythm is an American group from Clarksdale, Mississippi, formed in the late 1940s and led by Ike Turner until his death in 2007. It grew out of a large big band, the Tophatters, which sometimes had more than thirty members. When that group broke up, part of it continued as the Dukes of Swing and part under Turner as the Kings of Rhythm. In the beginning the group mainly played covers of popular jukebox hits and had a regular Wednesday night at the Harlem Theater in Clarksdale.

In 1951 the group recorded Rocket 88 at Sun Studios in Memphis, under the name Jackie Brenston and His Delta Cats. Brenston, the saxophonist, sang and suggested the subject, the new Oldsmobile Rocket 88, while Turner made the arrangement and the piano intro. The song reached the top of the R&B chart in June 1951 and is regarded as a candidate for the first rock and roll record. The success caused quarrels, because the members received little money and recognition.

In the 1960s the group became the band of the Ike & Tina Turner Revue. In the early 1970s it was called Family Vibes and made two albums, after which Turner took up the name again in 2001. The album Here and Now received a Grammy nomination, and with the group Turner made Risin' with the Blues (2006), which won a Grammy. In this way the name runs from the earliest rock and roll to the new century.
artiest/the-kings-of-rhythm.listen: Listen to Rocket 88 and notice the piano intro and the saxophone. Can you hear why this song is sometimes called the first rock and roll record?

artiest/the-kingsmen.text:
The Kingsmen were an American rock band from Portland, Oregon, in the 1960s. The teenagers Lynn Easton and Jack Ely began playing together in 1957, with Ely singing and playing guitar and Easton on drums. Mike Mitchell on guitar and Bob Nordby on bass joined, and in 1962 the schoolboy Don Gallucci joined the group as keyboardist. At first they mainly played at fashion shows and supermarket promotions and avoided rock songs.

In 1962, in a club in Seaside, Oregon, they saw the audience dance for hours to the version of Louie Louie by Rockin' Robin Roberts. Ely persuaded the band to learn the song. Because he had misheard the rhythm on a jukebox, he played a different beat from the original. Radio host Ken Chase became their manager. On 6 April 1963 they recorded a demo in an hour at a local studio, and from that came their version of Louie Louie, the song by the singer Richard Berry. The album The Kingsmen in Person spent more than a hundred weeks on the American charts. In total they had thirteen singles on the chart between 1963 and 1968.

The recording sounds raw, hasty and unintelligible. That is precisely why it became an example for garage bands that could make a hit without studio experience. Louie Louie remained a lasting classic.
artiest/the-kingsmen.listen: Listen to Louie Louie and notice the vocals, which are almost impossible to follow, and the little guitar riff that keeps returning. Can you hear that the band has more energy than precision?

artiest/the-kingston-trio.text:
The Kingston Trio was an American folk and pop group that helped set off the folk revival of the late 1950s. The group began as a nightclub act in the San Francisco area, with Dave Guard, Bob Shane and Nick Reynolds. Guard and Shane knew each other from the Punahou School in Honolulu, where they learned to play the ukulele. There they performed Tahitian, Hawaiian and calypso songs, and they admired Hawaiian slack key guitarists such as Gabby Pahinui.

In 1958 their first album came out, The Kingston Trio, with Tom Dooley. It became a hit and as a single sold more than three million copies. The group then released many albums, including Here We Go Again! and The Kingston Trio at Large in 1959, and Sold Out, String Along and The Last Month of the Year in 1960. Four of its albums were in the top ten best-selling records at the same time in November and December 1959, a record that stood for more than fifty years.

The group played acoustic folk with guitar, banjo and tight harmonies. Its sales figures showed that such music could work commercially, which opened the way for singer-songwriters, folk rock and Americana. That explains why the course mentions it in the story of the folk revival. The name still exists and is used by musicians who obtained the licence in 2017.
artiest/the-kingston-trio.listen: Listen to Tom Dooley and notice the harmony singing of the three men. Can you hear how the lyrics are told like a story, accompanied by little more than acoustic guitar and banjo?

artiest/the-kinks.text:
The Kinks formed in London in 1962 around the brothers Ray and Dave Davies from Muswell Hill. At home they heard the music hall of their parents and the jazz and early rock 'n' roll of their older sisters. With bassist Pete Quaife and drummer Mick Avory they formed the classic line-up: Ray sang and played rhythm guitar, Dave played lead guitar.

The breakthrough came in 1964 with You Really Got Me, the third single, which reached number 1 in England and was also a hit in America. All Day and All of the Night and Tired of Waiting for You followed. After problems during their American tour of 1965 they were banned from performing there for years. Ray Davies then turned his attention to England itself. Songs such as Dedicated Follower of Fashion, Sunny Afternoon (both 1966) and Waterloo Sunset (1967) and albums such as Face to Face (1966) and The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society (1968) describe English everyday life with a sharp, often mocking eye. In 1970 the band had another big hit with Lola.

Musically The Kinks began with American rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll, and later music hall, folk and country were added. The raw, distorted guitar sound of their early hits was seen as a forerunner of hard rock. The band lasted until 1997 and then split up because of tensions between the brothers. Van Halen, The Jam and The Pretenders covered their songs, and in the 1990s Britpop bands such as Blur and Oasis named them as an important influence.
artiest/the-kinks.listen: Listen to Waterloo Sunset (1967). Notice how calmly and almost contemplatively Ray Davies sings about a man looking at the Thames from his window, and how far that is from the raw guitar of their early hits.

artiest/the-klezmatics.text:
The Klezmatics are an American klezmer group from New York. The group began in 1986 in the East Village, with Frank London, Lorin Sklamberg, Margot Leverett, Alicia Svigals, David Licht and David Lindsay at the first rehearsal. Klezmer is the traditional music of the Eastern European Jews, and the Klezmatics became known above all by combining old Yiddish songs with contemporary music from all kinds of sources. They also sang in Aramaic and Bavarian. The members come from different worlds. One played jazz with Herbie Hancock and Chick Corea, another bluegrass and Celtic music.

Their albums include Shvaygn = Toyt from 1989, Rhythm + Jews from 1991, Jews With Horns from 1994, Possessed from 1997, The Well from 1998 and Rise Up! Shteyt oyf! from 2002. In 2006 came Wonder Wheel, with lyrics by Woody Guthrie from his archive. The group worked with among others Ferus Mustafov, Chava Alberstein, Arlo Guthrie and the Master Musicians of Jajouka, and with the poet Allen Ginsberg in Berlin. In 2010 the documentary The Klezmatics: On Holy Ground was released.

The line-up includes clarinet, trumpet, accordion, violin, bass and cimbalom. The Klezmatics showed that klezmer is not a museum piece but a living music, which belongs alongside rock and jazz. In this way they play a special role in the world music of the 1990s.
artiest/the-klezmatics.listen: Listen to Doyna and notice the clarinet and the violin that make the melody sound like singing. Can you hear how those instruments make the melody sound like a human voice?

artiest/the-knack.text:
The Knack was an American power pop band, formed in Los Angeles in 1978 by singer and rhythm guitarist Doug Fieger, lead guitarist Berton Averre, bassist Prescott Niles and drummer Bruce Gary. Fieger came from Oak Park near Detroit and had moved to Los Angeles after his previous band Sky, which was produced by Jimmy Miller, had no hits. With Averre he formed a songwriting duo. Within a few months of their first gig in June 1978 they were playing popular club shows on the Sunset Strip and a bidding war between record labels broke out. They signed with Capitol Records, for the largest sum in that label's history.

The debut album Get the Knack (1979) became one of the best-selling records of the year and spent five weeks at number one on the Billboard album chart. The single My Sharona, written by Fieger about Sharona Alperin, became the number one of 1979 in the United States. Good Girls Don't reached number one in Canada. The success provoked criticism: the 1960s retro look and the sleeve, which resembled Meet the Beatles!, led to the accusation that the band was copying The Beatles. Fieger did not entirely deny it and said that he wanted to let people who had not lived through the 1960s hear the sound of the British Invasion.

The following records, ...But the Little Girls Understand (1980) and Round Trip (1981), did less well, and in 1982 the group disbanded. Reunions and albums such as Serious Fun (1991), Zoom (1998) and Normal as the Next Guy (2001) followed later. After Fieger's death in 2010 it was definitively over.
artiest/the-knack.listen: Listen to My Sharona and notice the driving energy of the band and the simple, direct set-up. Can you hear why this is called a power pop record?

artiest/the-kyoto-kabuki-orchestra.text:
The Kyoto Kabuki Orchestra is the ensemble that performs the music for kabuki theatre. Little is known with certainty about the group itself, because the available source dealt with the director Tetsuji Takechi, who made influential experimental kabuki productions in the 1940s and 1950s. This text therefore mainly describes the music that can be heard in School of Rock.

Kabuki is a Japanese theatre genre in which dance, acting and music come together. The music is played live by an ensemble with vocals and shamisen, a three-stringed lute struck with a large plectrum, sometimes supplemented by flute and percussion. The singers tell the story or describe the feelings of the dancers. The shamisen sets the rhythm and creates the atmosphere. The piece Kagamijishi is a dance piece in which a dancer portrays a lion. Dōjōji belongs to a story about a woman and a temple bell, and is played here by the shamisen alone.

The sound is sharp and rhythmic. The shamisen strikes hard, abrupt tones, and the voice sounds high and tense. In this way the orchestra shows how the music of kabuki carries the tension of the stage.
artiest/the-kyoto-kabuki-orchestra.listen: Listen to the shamisen solo of Dōjōji. Notice the sharp, rhythmic attack of the strings and how the instrument sounds almost like a voice.

artiest/the-lau.text:
Thé Lau, in full Matheus Josephus Lau, was a Dutch singer, guitarist, lyricist and writer. He was born in 1952 in Bergen in North Holland and came from a family with a painter: his grandfather was also called Thé Lau. He played in various bands and was a member of Neerlands Hoop Express. In 1979 he founded The Scene, with himself as singer and guitarist. Their best-known songs are Blauw and Iedereen is van de wereld.

With The Scene Lau made solid guitar rock with Dutch lyrics, at a time when Nederpop was becoming increasingly self-confident. In 2003 he left the group. He then toured the theatres with keyboardist Jan-Peter Bast and in 2006 began the tour Tempel der liefde, together with Bast and the tango string quartet Pavadita. In 2007 The Scene got back together with Lau and three former members. His solo albums include De God van Nederland from 2002, Tempel der liefde from 2006 and Platina blues from 2014. In 2010 he topped the Dutch charts with the rapper Lange Frans with Zing voor me. In 2005 he wrote In vrijheid, a song that has since been widely sung every year around Liberation Day.

Lau also wrote books. He made his debut in 2000 with the short story collection De sterren van de hemel, published his lyrics in 2003 and wrote the novel Hemelrijk in 2004. In 2013 he was diagnosed with throat cancer. He died in 2015 in Amsterdam. His lyrics, plain, direct and often poetic, helped Dutch-language song to be taken seriously as rock music.
artiest/the-lau.listen: Listen to Blauw by The Scene. Notice the guitars, the voice of Thé Lau and how the lyrics stay Dutch without the music becoming soft or schlager-like.

artiest/the-lighthouse-all-stars.text:
The Lighthouse All-Stars were the house band of The Lighthouse, a jazz club at 30 Pier Avenue in Hermosa Beach, California. On 29 May 1949 owner John Levine let bassist and bandleader Howard Rumsey start a regular Sunday jam session, as a trial. It worked. Rumsey soon became manager of the club and put together a house band, the Lighthouse All-Stars.

Although visiting groups also played at the club, the group grew into an ensemble with a face of its own. Guest musicians included Chet Baker, Gerry Mulligan and Miles Davis. The longest-serving members were Bob Cooper on tenor saxophone, Conte Candoli on trumpet and Stan Levey on drums. The West Coast musicians Shorty Rogers, Bud Shank, Shelly Manne and Jimmy Giuffre were also regular guests in the early years, and in 1953 Max Roach was the regular drummer for a time. Recordings from 1953 include Sunday Jazz a la Lighthouse and, with Chet Baker and Miles Davis as guests, Witch Doctor and At Last!.

The club became an important place for live recordings. Cannonball Adderley, Art Blakey, Lee Morgan, The Jazz Crusaders and The Modern Jazz Quartet recorded albums there. Rumsey left in 1971 to open the club Concerts By The Sea in Redondo Beach. From 1981 the jazz policy was largely discontinued, but since the mid-1990s jazz has been slowly returning. The All-Stars belong to the West Coast jazz of the 1950s, the loose, relaxed side of jazz from California.
artiest/the-lighthouse-all-stars.listen: Listen to Witch Doctor by Chet Baker and the Lighthouse All-Stars and notice how the trumpet and the other soloists take turns being given room. Can you hear how relaxed it sounds?

artiest/the-london-metropolitan-orchestr.text:
The London Metropolitan Orchestra, abbreviated LMO, is a studio orchestra in London that specialises in recording film music. The orchestra has existed since 1994 and is led by conductor Andy Brown. It has worked for British and American film and television companies, such as the BBC, ITV and Walt Disney Studios. In 2021 the orchestra appointed Daisy Chute as choir director of the London Metropolitan Chorus.

The soundtracks the orchestra recorded include the Oscar-nominated films Don Juan DeMarco (1994) and Mr. Holland's Opus (1995), with music by Michael Kamen. The orchestra also recorded work by many other film composers, including Klaus Badelt, Danny Elfman, Elliot Goldenthal, Mark Isham, Howard Shore, Vangelis and Christopher Young. Well-known recordings are The Wings of the Dove by Ed Shearmur (1998), The Magic of Inspector Morse by Barrington Pheloung (2000), Mythodea by Vangelis (2001) and Band of Brothers by Michael Kamen (2003). Later came, among others, Stardust (2007), Still Alice (2014) and Shaun the Sheep Movie (2015), with music by Ilan Eshkeri.

A studio orchestra like this is seldom in the spotlight, but it plays a large part in how films sound. The musicians read the composer's score and record it, so that the music sounds equally rich in the film and on the soundtrack record. The LMO shows how important an orchestra behind the scenes can be in the pop and film world.
artiest/the-london-metropolitan-orchestr.listen: Listen to Mythodea by Vangelis, recorded in 2001 with the London Metropolitan Orchestra, and notice how the orchestra forms a large, cinematic whole. Can you hear which instruments carry the melody?

artiest/the-mamas-en-the-papas.text:
The Mamas & the Papas were an American folk rock group that recorded and performed from 1965 to 1968, with a short reunion in 1971. They were formed in New York by John Phillips and his wife Michelle Phillips, the Canadian Denny Doherty and Cass Elliot. Elliot was the last to join. The name was inspired by the Hells Angels, whose female circle was called mamas. The sound revolved around the vocal harmonies that John Phillips arranged. He wrote the songs and led the group. He adapted folk to the new beat of the early 1960s.

In the summer of 1965 they rehearsed in the Virgin Islands, where they played electric for the first time. They then travelled to Los Angeles for an audition with Lou Adler of Dunhill Records. Their second single, California Dreamin', was released in December 1965 and reached number four in the United States. In 1966 the albums If You Can Believe Your Eyes and Ears and The Mamas & the Papas were released, in 1967 Deliver and in 1968 The Papas & the Mamas. The group had seventeen singles, six of them in the Billboard top ten.

In 1968 the group split up, and in 1971 the album People Like Us followed. Cass Elliot died in 1974. In 1998 the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, where they performed together one more time. The group is regarded as a defining force in the counterculture of the 1960s. Their harmonies showed how folk could sound in a pop world that had just been changed by the Beatles.
artiest/the-mamas-en-the-papas.listen: Listen to California Dreamin' and notice how the four voices together form a single harmony. Can you hear which voice carries the melody and which voices sing around it?

artiest/the-manhattan-transfer.text:
The Manhattan Transfer was an American vocal group, founded in New York in 1969 by Tim Hauser and named after the novel by John Dos Passos. The first line-up made one album, Jukin' in 1971, and broke up in 1973. Hauser then formed a new group with Alan Paul, Janis Siegel and Laurel Massé. This one leaned more towards vocal jazz and swing, and signed with Atlantic Records. The debut album The Manhattan Transfer was released in 1975, with Operator and a vocalese version of Tuxedo Junction. Coming Out followed in 1976, with Chanson d'Amour, a number one in the United Kingdom and Ireland.

After a car accident involving Massé, Cheryl Bentyne took her place in 1979. The album Extensions brought Twilight Zone/Twilight Tone and a version of Birdland, an instrumental piece by Weather Report, with lyrics by Jon Hendricks of Lambert, Hendricks and Ross. Birdland became one of the most popular jazz records of the year in 1980 and won a Grammy. Later came, among others, Mecca for Moderns in 1981, Vocalese in 1985 and Brasil in 1987. In total they won eleven Grammys. The group brought its career to an end in 2023.

The Manhattan Transfer showed how a vocal group can take over a jazz piece: the voices play the instrument parts, and put lyrics beneath them. That is called vocalese. They combined jazz, swing, rhythm and blues and pop, and in this way brought jazz to a wide audience.
artiest/the-manhattan-transfer.listen: Listen to Birdland by The Manhattan Transfer. Notice how the four voices take over the parts of a band, and how the lyrics follow the melody of the original.

artiest/the-mar-keys.text:
The Mar-Keys were an American studio band for Stax Records in Memphis, Tennessee, formed in 1958 as the label's first house band. Their accompaniment formed the basis of the early Stax sound of the 1960s. The members began in high school as the Royal Spades. The mother of tenor saxophonist Packy Axton, Estelle Axton, ran the label Satellite, the forerunner of Stax, with her brother, and she persuaded the group to take the name Mar-Keys.

Their best-known recording is Last Night from 1961, a song carried by organ and saxophone. It reached number three in the United States and sold more than a million copies. On that recording Steve Cropper, normally a guitarist, played second keyboards, because producer Chips Moman did not want a guitar. Also heard were Packy Axton, trumpeter Wayne Jackson and Jerry Lee Smoochy Smith. A second hit never came, but the name lived on.

The originally white group was replaced in the studio by session musicians. As a result the name Mar-Keys became the name of Stax's mixed house band, with a changing line-up. Those players, including Steve Cropper, Donald Duck Dunn and Al Jackson Jr., accompanied dozens of artists, among them Otis Redding, Carla Thomas and Wilson Pickett. In 1962 Cropper, Jackson and Booker T. Jones also began recording as Booker T. & the M.G.'s. Songs with horns were released under the name Mar-Keys, songs without horns under that of the M.G.'s. The Mar-Keys therefore belong to the foundations of Memphis soul.
artiest/the-mar-keys.listen: Listen to Last Night and notice the organ and the saxophone, which together carry the melody. Can you hear how little is needed to carry the song?

artiest/the-marvelettes.text:
The Marvelettes were an American girl group, formed in 1960 at Inkster High School in Inkster, Michigan, near Detroit. The fifteen-year-old Gladys Horton founded the group with Katherine Anderson, Georgeanna Tillman, Juanita Cowart and Georgia Dobbins. Dobbins was replaced by Wanda Young before the group got its first contract. After a talent contest they were given an audition at Motown, where Berry Gordy asked them to come back with a song of their own. Dobbins was given an unfinished blues song by William Garrett and rewrote it overnight into Please Mr. Postman.

Gordy gave them the name Marvelettes and signed them in July 1961 to Motown's Tamla branch. Please Mr. Postman was released in August 1961 and was number one in December. It was one of the first number one singles by a female vocal group and the first by a Motown act. Dobbins gave the song the teenage sound of doo-wop. The group suffered from little promotion by Motown, health problems and substance use. Cowart left in 1963, Tillman in 1965 and Horton in 1967. In 1966 a comeback followed with Don't Mess with Bill.

In 1969 the group stopped performing and a year later it ceased, after the album The Return of the Marvelettes, on which only Wanda Young, under the name Wanda Rogers, could be heard. The Marvelettes opened the way for the Motown girl groups that came after them.
artiest/the-marvelettes.listen: Listen to Please Mr. Postman and notice the singing of the group and the simple, direct lyrics. Can you hear the doo-wop in the singing?

artiest/the-memphis-horns.text:
The Memphis Horns were an American horn section, who became known through their many recordings for Stax Records. The duo consisted of trumpeter Wayne Jackson and tenor saxophonist Andrew Love and was described as an offshoot of the Mar-Keys. Jackson played with the Mar-Keys as a schoolboy, Love played in his father's church and joined the Stax house band in 1965. They clicked quickly. In 1969 Stax asked them to work only there, but they refused and founded The Memphis Horns, in order to be able to offer their sound to everyone.

They also worked at Royal Studio and American Sound Studio in Memphis, at Atlantic Records in New York and at FAME Studio in Muscle Shoals. They played on almost every Stax recording with horns, for Isaac Hayes, Otis Redding, Rufus Thomas and Sam & Dave, and on more than a hundred hits by others, such as (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay by Otis Redding, Let's Stay Together by Al Green and Suspicious Minds by Elvis Presley. In the 1970s they worked with among others Aretha Franklin, Rod Stewart and Neil Diamond, and toured with The Doobie Brothers. Later they played on records by the Robert Cray Band and on Rattle and Hum by U2. In 1992 their own album Flame Out was released.

Love stopped in 2004. In 2012 the Memphis Horns received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. They show how important the horn section is to the sound of soul.
artiest/the-memphis-horns.listen: Listen to (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay by Otis Redding and notice the horns that complement the vocals. What would be missing if the horns were gone?

artiest/the-modernaires.text:
The Modernaires were an American vocal group, best known for their appearances in the 1940s with the orchestra of Glenn Miller. They began in 1934 as a trio of school friends from Buffalo, New York: Hal Dickinson, Chuck Goldstein and Bill Conway. After appearing on the radio in Buffalo they went to New York and were given a 26-week contract on CBS radio. With Ralph Brewster they became a quartet and appeared with among others the orchestras of Fred Waring, Charlie Barnet, George Hall and Paul Whiteman.

In October 1940 Glenn Miller asked them to record It's Make Believe Ballroom Time, and in January 1941 they became a permanent part of his orchestra. Singer Paula Kelly, who was married to Dickinson, joined later, after which the group became a quintet. After the film Sun Valley Serenade the group had ten hits in 1941. Well-known songs by Miller and The Modernaires are Chattanooga Choo Choo with Tex Beneke, Perfidia, Elmer's Tune, Serenade in Blue and (I've Got a Gal In) Kalamazoo. Chattanooga Choo Choo was the first gold record ever, with more than a million copies sold.

After Miller's disappearance they recorded vocal versions of his instrumental hits, such as Moonlight Serenade and A String of Pearls. In 1945 they had their first top twenty hit with There! I've Said It Again. In the 1960s they sang the theme song of the TV series Hazel. In this way the group belongs to the colour of the big-band era, in which singers used harmony singing as an instrument of its own.
artiest/the-modernaires.listen: Listen to Chattanooga Choo Choo with Glenn Miller and The Modernaires and notice how the group places the vocals as an instrument of its own within the sound of the orchestra. Where do the voices come in?

artiest/the-moody-blues.text:
The Moody Blues were an English rock band, formed in Birmingham in May 1964 by Ray Thomas, Mike Pinder, Graeme Edge, Denny Laine and Clint Warwick. The name referred to the brewery Mitchells & Butlers, which the band hoped would sponsor it, to the jazz piece Mood Indigo by Duke Ellington and to the rhythm and blues the group was playing at the time. At the end of 1964 the band reached number 1 in England with Go Now. After that the success stopped, and in 1966 Warwick and Laine left. Justin Hayward and John Lodge took their places.

With the new line-up the music changed. Pinder switched from piano to Mellotron. In 1967 Days of Future Passed was released, an album that combined rock with classical music, recorded with the London Festival Orchestra. It produced Nights in White Satin and Tuesday Afternoon and is regarded as one of the first successful concept albums. On the following records, from In Search of the Lost Chord (1968) to Seventh Sojourn (1972), the Mellotron replaced the orchestra. The songs often flowed into one another. In the 1980s the band acquired a synth-pop sound, with hits such as Your Wildest Dreams.

The Moody Blues began as a beat group, but grew into one of the pioneers of art rock and progressive rock. The Mellotron gave the band a sound of its own: a keyboard instrument with tapes of real strings and flutes, with which a small rock band could sound like an orchestra.
artiest/the-moody-blues.listen: Listen to Nights in White Satin and notice the string sounds. They come from the Mellotron, which plays a tape with a recording for every key. Can you hear how that sound floats a little and sounds different from a real string orchestra?

artiest/the-mothers-of-invention.text:
The Mothers of Invention, the Mothers for short, were an American rock band from California. It began as an R&B group under the name Soul Giants. When Ray Collins asked guitarist Frank Zappa to take over the band, he insisted on playing original material. One of the members left as a result, and on Mother's Day 1965 the band changed its name to the Mothers. The record company wanted a different name, and according to Zappa they became the Mothers of Invention out of necessity, after the proverb that necessity is the mother of invention.

The group attracted attention in the Los Angeles underground. Producer Tom Wilson, who had also produced Bob Dylan and Simon and Garfunkel, saw them play in 1966 and brought them to Verve Records. There the double album Freak Out! was released in 1966. Absolutely Free followed in 1967, Cruising with Ruben and the Jets and We're Only in It for the Money in 1968 and Uncle Meat in 1969. Zappa disbanded the group in 1969 and put together a new line-up in 1970, with among others Mark Volman and Howard Kaylan. After an attack by a member of the audience in London at the end of 1971 Zappa was seriously injured. In 1973 he formed a final line-up, and the last album under the name was Bongo Fury in 1975, with Captain Beefheart.

The music of the Mothers revolved around sound experiments, satire, playful sleeves and elaborate live shows. What the Beatles did in 1967 with concept albums and studio effects had already been prepared by Freak Out! and the Beach Boys' Pet Sounds, both from 1966. Their influence lay above all in the freedom: a pop album could be a joke, a protest and avant-garde all at once.
artiest/the-mothers-of-invention.listen: Listen to Trouble Every Day by The Mothers of Invention. Notice the bluesy accompaniment and the lyrics, in which Zappa comments on the riots in Watts.

artiest/the-motions.text:
The Motions was a nederbeat band from The Hague, formed in 1964 by Henk Smitskamp on bass guitar, Robbie van Leeuwen on guitar, Rudy Bennett as singer and Sieb Warner on drums. Bennett and Van Leeuwen came from Ritchie & the Ricochets, who had played in August 1964 before the Rolling Stones at the Kurhaus in Scheveningen. The band existed until 1970 and is regarded as the first nederbeat group to reach the hit parade. That happened in early 1965 with the first single It's Gone, which reached number 39 in the Veronica Top 40.

In 1965 came the first album, Introduction to the Motions, with eleven songs by Van Leeuwen, and the first big hit, Wasted Words. It was inspired by the protest song. In 1966 Why Don't You Take It, Every Step I Take and It's the Same Old Song followed, with the album Their Own Way. Bennett had a solo success in 1967 with How Can We Hang On to a Dream.

Van Leeuwen left in March 1967 and founded Shocking Blue, known for Venus. Gerard Romeijn took his place. With Impressions of Wonderful (1967) the band joined flower power, and the magazine Hitweek called the album the Dutch Sgt. Pepper's. In 1969 Electric Baby followed and a short trip to the United States, without a breakthrough. In 1970 the album Sensation was released, after which the group disbanded.
artiest/the-motions.listen: Listen to Wasted Words and notice the guitar and the vocals. This is a Dutch beat band from 1965: what do you hear of the beat of that time?

artiest/the-music-improvisation-company.text:
The Music Improvisation Company was a British free-improvisation group that began around 1968 and whose first album came out in 1970 on ECM Records. The line-up consisted of saxophonist Evan Parker, guitarist Derek Bailey, Hugh Davies with home-built electronic instruments and percussionist Jamie Muir. On two tracks guest singer Christine Jeffrey sang along. The record was recorded in three days in August 1970, with Manfred Eicher as producer.

The music was deliberately not written in any existing style. The musicians knew jazz well, but they used whatever element they wanted, and gave it shape in the moment. The result sounded dissonant and disjointed, and was ahead of its time in free improvisation. One critic called Evan Parker's bubbling outbursts of indeterminate melody the highlight, while Bailey chose a more anonymous approach, cutting rapidly in and out of the music. In 1976 the compilation album 1968 - 1971 was also released.

The group is important to the history of improvised music in Europe. Many of the musicians went on to play a major part in free improvisation. In pop history it stands at the edge, with the experimental music that lets rock, jazz and electronics come together without fixed rules. Dragon Path is a good place to try this out.
artiest/the-music-improvisation-company.listen: Listen to Dragon Path and notice how no single instrument takes the lead. Try to hear when the saxophone, the guitar and the electronics respond to one another, and when each goes its own way.

artiest/the-new-orleans-wanderers.text:
The New Orleans Wanderers was the name under which Lil Hardin recorded in 1926 with members of Louis Armstrong's Hot Five, during a session for Columbia. Armstrong himself could not take part, because he was under contract to Okeh, although he did contribute to three of the four songs. His place was taken by cornettist George Mitchell.

The line-up otherwise consisted of Lil Hardin on piano, Kid Ory on trombone, Johnny St. Cyr on banjo and Johnny Dodds on clarinet. All the songs were written by Louis Armstrong. The session took place in Chicago on 13 July 1926 and produced four songs under this name: Gate Mouth, Too Tight, Perdido Street Blues and Papa Dip. The next day the same musicians recorded four other songs, which were released under the name New Orleans Bootblacks: I Can't Say, Mixed Salad, Mad Dog and Flat Foot.

In this way the New Orleans Wanderers show how names and contracts worked in early jazz. The same players worked under different names for different labels, and the music comes from the New Orleans jazz of the 1920s, played by the circle around Armstrong. The songs were later also released in England, including in the Columbia Swing Music Series.
artiest/the-new-orleans-wanderers.listen: Listen to Perdido Street Blues and notice the interplay between the clarinet, the trombone and the cornet. Which instruments do you recognise and what does each of them do?

artiest/the-notorious-b-i-g.text:
The Notorious B.I.G., also known as Biggie Smalls, was an American rapper and lyricist. His name was Christopher George Latore Wallace and he was born in 1972 in Brooklyn, New York, the only child of Jamaican parents. His father left the family when he was almost three, and his mother raised him alone. At Westinghouse High School he got the nickname Big. In 1993 he was the first artist to sign with Sean Combs's Bad Boy Records, and he stood out for his guest appearances on other people's singles.

His debut album Ready to Die from 1994 contained the singles Juicy, Big Poppa and One More Chance. It made him the central figure of East Coast hip hop, at a time when the West Coast dominated the genre. In 1995 he was named Rapper of the Year at the Billboard Music Awards. He was also involved in the growing rivalry between East and West Coast, among other things in a feud with his former friend Tupac Shakur. Shakur was shot dead in Las Vegas in September 1996. Six months later, on 9 March 1997, Wallace himself was shot dead in Los Angeles in a drive-by shooting. Two weeks later the double album Life After Death was released, with Hypnotize and Mo Money Mo Problems.

Wallace was known for his relaxed, loose way of rapping, which contrasted with the often grim content of his lyrics. His music was half autobiographical and told of poverty and crime, but also of excess and partying. He is widely seen as one of the best rappers ever, and in 2020 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. His death showed how deep the rivalry in hip hop could go.
artiest/the-notorious-b-i-g.listen: Listen to Juicy by The Notorious B.I.G. Notice the calm, almost storytelling way of rapping and the story of the road from poverty to success.

artiest/the-o-jays.text:
The O'Jays are an American R&B group from Canton, Ohio. They formed in the summer of 1958 at Canton McKinley High School, with Eddie Levert, Walter Lee Williams, William Powell, Bobby Massey and Bill Isles. At first they were called The Mascots and then The Triumphs. In 1963 they took the name The O'Jays, in honour of the Cleveland radio DJ Eddie O'Jay. Their first chart entry was Lonely Drifter in 1963, and shortly afterwards their debut album Comin' Through came out. In the 1960s they made dozens of singles, but they did not reach the American top forty.

The turning point came in 1971, when the producers Gamble and Huff signed them to their label Philadelphia International. By then they were a trio, after Isles and Massey had left. In 1972, with Back Stabbers, they were at the forefront of Philadelphia soul. The following year Love Train reached number one on the American Hot 100. They were inducted into the Vocal Group Hall of Fame in 2004, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005 and the Rhythm and Blues Music Hall of Fame in 2013.

Philadelphia soul sounds rich and warm, with strings, brass and a tight rhythm section over which the voices sing. The O'Jays gave that sound a message, with calls for unity as in Love Train. In this way they belong to the groups that prepared the way for soul and disco.
artiest/the-o-jays.listen: Listen to Love Train and notice the chorus, in which the whole group sings along. Can you hear how rhythm and strings together build a feeling of moving forward?

artiest/the-offspring.text:
The Offspring is an American rock band from Garden Grove, California, formed in 1984 under the name Manic Subsidal. The group now consists of singer and guitarist Dexter Holland, guitarist Noodles, bassist Todd Morse, Jonah Nimoy and drummer Brandon Pertzborn. They first gained a local following with their album The Offspring from 1989 and the EP Baghdad from 1991. They then signed with the independent label Epitaph Records and made Ignition in 1992 and Smash in 1994.

Smash contained the first big hit, Come Out and Play, and is regarded as one of the best-selling albums on an independent label. It brought punk rock back to the general public. In 1996 the group signed with Columbia Records, which released Ixnay on the Hombre in 1997. The album Americana from 1998 produced Pretty Fly (For a White Guy), Why Don't You Get a Job? and The Kids Aren't Alright, hits on radio and MTV. In 2008 Rise and Fall, Rage and Grace was released, with You're Gonna Go Far, Kid.

The music of The Offspring is fast, melodic punk rock, with heavy guitars and an easy-to-follow chorus. In the 1990s the band played a key role in the renewed success of punk. Self Esteem from Smash lets you hear how that style sounded.
artiest/the-offspring.listen: Listen to Self Esteem and notice the tempo. Can you hear how guitars and drums drive the song forward?

artiest/the-outsiders.text:
The Outsiders was a nederbeat band from Amsterdam led by singer Wally Tax. In its best-known line-up the group consisted of Tax on vocals, Ronnie Splinter and Tom Krabbendam on guitar, Appie Rammers on bass and Leendert Buzz Busch on drums. Frank Beek played bass in 1968 and 1969. They were most popular in the Netherlands from 1965 to 1967, but released records until 1969. Nederbeat was the Dutch variant of the beat music that arose after the British Invasion.

Unlike many European bands that followed the Beatles, the Outsiders took as their example rougher British groups, such as the Pretty Things and the Rolling Stones. On 26 March 1966 they played in 's-Hertogenbosch as support act for the Stones' second Dutch concert. The group released thirteen singles, including Summer Is Here in 1967, which reached the Dutch top ten. Its albums were Outsiders and the singles compilation Songbook in 1967, and C.Q. in 1968. The latter sold poorly, but is now regarded as a masterpiece of psychedelic rock and garage rock. Unusually for the time the band did not record covers.

After the Summer of Love many nederbeat bands fell out of favour. The Outsiders tried to keep attention with style experiments and publicity stunts, but lost fans. In the autumn of 1969 Splinter stopped and the group fell apart. Tax and Busch then formed Tax Free. In 1997 a reunion tour followed, and Tax died in 2005. Today the group is regarded as a special example of garage rock from the Netherlands, and its work is also being rediscovered outside the Netherlands.
artiest/the-outsiders.listen: Listen to Summer Is Here by The Outsiders. Notice the voice of Wally Tax and the rough, guitar-driven sound that is further from the Beatles than from the Stones.

artiest/the-partridge-family.text:
The Partridge Family was a fictional pop group in an American musical comedy series on the ABC network, devised by Bernard Slade. The series ran from September 1970 to March 1974. It revolves around the widow Shirley Partridge, played by Shirley Jones, and her children, including Keith, played by David Cassidy, Laurie and Danny. Together with manager Reuben Kincaid they make a hit and go on tour in a bus painted with Mondrian patterns. The family was loosely based on the Cowsills, a real family band of the late 1960s.

The music, however, was not an act. In the early days the actors pretended to sing while records by session musicians were played. Shirley Jones was initially the only one who really sang. After Cassidy had shown music producer Wes Farrell that he could sing, he was allowed to record his own parts. For the rest, well-known studio musicians played, now known as the Wrecking Crew, and the Ron Hicklin Singers sang the backing vocals. The sound of the Partridge Family was therefore a studio creation.

The first single I Think I Love You, written by Tony Romeo, came out in 1970. It spent three weeks at number one on the American Hot 100 and sold more than five million copies. With that the Partridge Family became, after a few other cartoon characters, the third fictional artist with a number one. The albums followed one another quickly, from The Partridge Family Album in 1970 to Crossword Puzzle in 1973. Cassidy felt trapped by fame and broke with his wholesome image in 1972. The group shows how pop could be made as a product: a television family, a studio band and an idol.
artiest/the-partridge-family.listen: Listen to I Think I Love You by The Partridge Family. Notice how polished the production sounds, with Cassidy's voice in front and the many backing voices behind.

artiest/the-peech-boys.text:
The Peech Boys, also known as the New York Citi Peech Boys, were an American group around Bernard Fowler, Steven Brown, Robert Kasper, Darryl Short, Larry Levan and Michael de Benedictus. The group arose at the Paradise Garage, under the influence of DJ Larry Levan. They released only four twelve-inch records. They signed with West End Records, then with Island Records, and split up in 1984.

Their best-known song is Don't Make Me Wait from 1982. It became one of the early hits of the New York house and garage scene, because Levan played it at the Paradise Garage. It was also their only entry on the British chart, in November 1982. The track sounds tight and dance-like. The music sits between disco, post-disco and what would later be called house.

The Peech Boys are important because they let us hear how New York club culture sounded around 1982, before house broke through from Chicago. The song is an example of how a DJ and a group together devised a sound that worked on the dance floor. As a result they stand in the history of dance music between disco and house.
artiest/the-peech-boys.listen: Listen to Don't Make Me Wait and notice the rhythm section. Can you hear how the vocals rise above it?

artiest/the-penguins.text:
The Penguins were an American doo-wop group from Los Angeles, active in the 1950s and early 1960s. The original members were tenor Cleveland Duncan, Curtis Williams as baritone and bass, tenor Dexter Tisby and baritone Bruce Tate. Duncan and Williams had been at Fremont High School together. At the end of 1953 they founded the group. The name came from Willie the Penguin, the cartoon character in the advertising for Kool cigarettes, and suited a group that thought of itself as cool. Many doo-wop groups then bore a bird name, such as The Orioles, The Flamingos and The Crows.

In 1954 Dootone Records released the single Hey Senorita, but a radio DJ turned the record over and played the B-side: Earth Angel. That song, which Williams had worked on with Gaynel Hodge, spent three weeks at the top of the Billboard R&B chart in early 1955. By 1966 four million copies had been sold. It remained their only big hit.

Earth Angel is a quiet, swaying song with a slow piano accompaniment and the soft harmony singing for which doo-wop is known. The group played a style between rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll. The song was one of the first R&B songs to also reach the pop charts, and shows how black vocal groups found a wider audience in the 1950s.
artiest/the-penguins.listen: Listen to Earth Angel and notice the slow triplet patterns on the piano. Can you hear how the lead and the backing singers alternate with one another?
